## Introduction

Multicellular organisms rely on coordinated cell--cell communication (CCC) to guide development, maintain homeostasis, and mount immune responses\ [@doi:10.1016/j.semcancer.2023.07.001].
This communication is mediated by a diverse molecular ensemble, including ligands, receptors, chemokines, hormones, and structural proteins\ [@doi:10.1016/j.semcancer.2023.07.001; @doi:10.1038/s41392-024-01888-z].
CCC occurs when extracellular ligand--receptor (LR) interactions trigger intracellular cascades, often altering gene expression to regulate cellular behavior and function.
By mapping how diseases disrupt these pathways, we can characterize the specific cellular coordination that drives and defines pathological states.

To better understand how cells interact, researchers have developed computational techniques to infer CCC from transcriptomic data\ [@doi:10.1038/s41576-020-00292-x; @doi:10.1038/s41467-022-30755-0].
These methods typically leverage single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to identify the co-expression of LR gene pairs documented in curated databases\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9; @doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btab036].
This approach hinges on the central assumption that transcript levels accurately reflect functional protein abundance, which in turn determines the probability of interaction.
While this is a simplified premise, it allows for the high-throughput screening of thousands of possible interactions, providing a data-driven way to prioritize specific communication events for experimental validation\ [@doi:10.1038/s41596-024-01045-4; @doi:10.1093/bib/bbaf280].
Initial tools such as CellPhoneDB and CellChat score communication based on ligand and receptor expression, then use statistical tests to compare those scores against a null distribution formed by permuting cell labels\ [@doi:10.1038/s41596-020-0292-x; @doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9].
Originally designed to merely detect the presence of active signaling pathways, these foundational tools have since inspired a diverse analytical toolkit capable of addressing increasingly complex biological questions\ [@doi:10.1038/s41576-023-00685-8].

A critical objective of CCC analysis is to understand how cellular interactions shift across biological contexts, such as disease states, developmental stages, treatment groups, or individual patients\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2; @doi:10.1038/s41467-017-02391-6; @doi:10.1073/pnas.1918937117; @doi:10.1186/1471-2105-12-19].
By mapping alterations in LR activity, researchers can pinpoint the communication programs that drive phenotypic outcomes and identify potential therapeutic targets.
The most direct strategies, such as scDiffCom, CrossTalkeR, and NATMI, contrast two conditions at a time to identify interactions associated with disease or phenotypic changes\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x; @doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btab370; @doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18873-z].
However, pairwise comparison tools ignore variation between individual samples and miss communication patterns that span many conditions.

Multi-condition CCC-inference tools generally fall into two primary categories: matrix-based and tensor-based methods.
Matrix-based strategies, including DIALOGUE, MultiNicheNet, and Multicellular Factor Analysis, flatten multi-dimensional data into two dimensions, typically with samples as rows and sender--receiver features as columns\ [@doi:10.1038/s41587-022-01288-0; @doi:10.7554/eLife.93161; @doi:10.1101/2023.06.13.544751].
While these methods can identify statistically significant LR pairs, flattening forces distinct modes to share rows or columns, which confounds patterns of variation present in individual dimensions.
In contrast, tensor-based methods like Tensor-cell2cell, scTensor, STACCato, and scITD organize the data into three- or four-dimensional tensors to preserve the data's higher-order structure, which allows these methods to identify coordinated changes in CCC across conditions and cell types\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2; @doi:10.1016/j.ajhg.2026.05.005; @doi:10.1038/s41587-024-02411-z; @doi:10.1186/s12859-023-05490-y].
To extract these insights, tensor-based tools employ factorization techniques, such as Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD), which model the tensor as a sum of rank-one components to reveal distinct signaling patterns\ [@doi:10.1137/07070111X; @doi:10.1016/j.cels.2024.07.004].

Despite their advantages, current tensor-based methods rely on pseudobulked single-cell data, which poses a significant limitation.
Because standard decompositions like CPD require data dimensions to be strictly aligned (i.e., \"sender cell type 1\" must match across all conditions), researchers are forced to aggregate single-cell measurements based on discrete cell-type labels.
This approach relies on the reductive assumption that a cell can be fully defined by a single label\ [@doi:10.1093/bib/bbaf280].
In reality, cells are multifaceted entities that often hold simultaneous identities, blending stable lineage markers with transient functional states driven by their immediate environment\ [@doi:10.1038/s41583-019-0125-5; @doi:10.1101/2022.06.03.494765; @doi:10.1186/s13148-022-01253-3].
Furthermore, the process of annotation itself is fraught with challenges; cell-type labels are inevitably incomplete or inaccurate, particularly when researchers attempt to define the fine-grained cell types needed to capture subtle heterogeneity.
Pseudobulking also obscures the functional diversity that drives cellular communication by merging subpopulations that may participate in entirely distinct signaling programs.
A separate class of methods, such as Scriabin, NICHES, DeepCOLOR, DeepTalk, and SPRUCE, avoids pseudobulking by scoring interactions directly between individual cells\ [@doi:10.1038/s41587-023-01782-z; @doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btac775; @doi:10.1016/j.cels.2024.01.007; @doi:10.1038/s41467-024-51329-2; @doi:10.1016/j.isci.2023.106025].
However, these single-cell methods do not model coordinated communication changes across many conditions, a central strength of tensor-based methods.
Therefore, there is a pressing need for a framework that can interpret the multi-dimensional nature of CCC across conditions while preserving the single-cell resolution necessary to capture complex, overlapping cellular identities.

Here, we present CCC-RISE, a tensor method designed to bring single-cell resolution to multi-condition CCC analyses.
CCC-RISE builds upon the Reduction and Insight in Single-cell Exploration (RISE) method, which utilizes PARAFAC2 to analyze scRNA-seq data without requiring pre-defined cell-type labels or aggregation\ [@doi:10.1016/j.cels.2025.101294].
PARAFAC2 aligns cells across conditions by projecting each cell onto a shared set of latent expression programs, termed "eigen-states," that capture the dominant axes of transcriptional variation common to all samples.
Further, each cell is defined by its projection onto every eigen-state, so PARAFAC2 preserves continuous variation rather than forcing discrete cell assignments.
PARAFAC2 thus supplies what tensor-based methods obtain through pseudobulking: an aligned cell dimension that represents the same gene programs in every condition.
Although other dimensionality reduction methods could supply these single-cell embeddings, RISE's eigen-states exhibit two key advantages.
First, PARAFAC2 has a unique solution, so eigen-states represent a non-arbitrary choice of basis for LR interaction scoring\ [@{doi:10.1002/(SICI)1099-128X(199905/08)13:3/4<295::AID-CEM547>3.0.CO;2-Y}].
Second, eigen-states are defined by explicit cell and gene weights, so LR interactions can be traced back to individual cells\ [@doi:10.1016/j.cels.2025.101294].
Here, we apply standard CCC scoring and tensor factorization to RISE's eigen-states to identify core communication programs across varying conditions while preserving the ability to interpret these signals at the single-cell level.
We then compare CCC-RISE with tensor-based methods that aggregate cells by annotation to identify which kinds of communication programs are obscured by pseudobulking.
